title: The Ringelmann Effect in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Scaling Law for Effective Team Size
claim: Collective team size saturates far below nominal size, and the interaction mode determines which scaling regime a system falls into.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side; line plot left, parameter scatter right with shaded regime bands
description: Two plots sit side by side. Panel A is a line plot of answer-level effective team size against nominal team size N, from 1 to 30. A dashed gray diagonal marks the independent-voter ideal, and a pink shaded wedge beneath it is labeled as the departure from that ideal. Green self-correction and blue noise-placebo curves nearly overlap and rise sublinearly to about 6 at N=30. A red debate curve is nearly flat at about 1.8. Direct labels at the right end of the curves give the endpoint values. Panel B is a scatter of the fitted exponent β against the ceiling parameter c, drawn over horizontal bands for near-linear growth (green), sublinear (yellow) and near-saturation (pink). Green and blue dots cluster near β≈0.25, and the red dot sits at the bottom. The eye goes first to the diverging red and green/blue curves in A.
caption: Effective team size saturates and the regime is set by collaboration mode (Qwen2.5-7B $\times$ GSM-Hard). A: Answer-level effective team size $N_eff^{ans}$ vs.\ nominal $N$. Self-correction and noise placebo grow sublinearly toward $N_eff \approx 6$ at $N{=}30$. Debate flattens at $N_eff \approx 1.8$. The dashed line marks the independent-voter ideal $N_eff = N$, and the shaded gap is the departure of the observed team from that ideal. B: Fitted Ringelmann parameters $(c, \beta)$ for the three modes. Self-correction and noise sit in the sublinear band ($\beta \approx 0.25$), debate sits in the hard-ceiling band ($\beta \approx 0$).
abstract: Inference-time multi-agent LLM scaling lacks a shared unit: counting nominal agents conflates cost with independent evidence. We derive a two-parameter scaling law $R(N) = N_\text{eff}/N = 1/(1+c(N-1)N^{-Î²})$ where the regime exponent $Î²$ classifies any configuration into one of three asymptotic regimes -- hard-ceiling at $1/c$ ($Î²= 0$), sublinear at $N^Î²/c$ ($0 < Î²< 1$), or linear ($Î²\ge 1$), and a mean-field theorem predicts that peer count $k$ and rounds $Ï$ during agent debate enter the dynamics only through their product $kÏ$. The law applies at two levels: answer diversity and correctness redundancy. Across 44 (model $\times$ task $\times$ condition) cells spanning peer debate, self-correction, random-noise placebo, self-consistency, three open-weight families (Qwen, Llama, Ministral) at scales from 7B to 32B with a frontier API check (Gemini), thinking models, heterogeneous teams, and sparse communication, the functional form fits every condition at $R^2 > 0.99$; only $(c, Î²)$ shifts. On free-form math, dense peer influence collapses the answer-level regime from sublinear into hard-ceiling; correctness-level fits remain hard-ceiling throughout. Three findings have practical implications. \emph{(i)}~Thirty dense debating agents produce no more answer diversity than one on MMLU-Hard. \emph{(ii)}~A noise placebo tracks self-correction on free-form math and at $4\times$ scale, so within homogeneous teams the gain commonly attributed to ``debate'' comes from re-evaluation, not peer content. \emph{(iii)}~A single $N \le 5$ pilot predicts the $N=30$ structural ceiling, and within the configurations tested only architectural diversity (heterogeneous teams) lowers $c$ and escapes the hard-ceiling regime, communication-mode interventions do not.
